high-seas.essay:
The high seas are the part of the ocean beyond every country's coastal zones. The ocean covers more than 70% of Earth's surface. About 58.6% of the sea surface is high seas, by the calculation of MarineRegions, a marine geography database, which works out at roughly 40% of the whole planet. Parliamentarians for Global Action, an advocacy group, gives 43% of Earth's surface in one place and about half in another, because the figure depends on how the area is defined. Either way, this is the largest part of the planet that no government owns, which is why people who want to start a new society keep looking at it.

The rules come from the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans. It has been in effect since 16 November 1994 and has 172 members. The United States has not joined it. The high-seas rules cover all sea outside a country's exclusive economic zone (its coastal resource zone, up to 200 nautical miles or about 370 km), its territorial sea (the belt next to its coast), its internal waters and the waters between the islands of an island nation (Article 86).

These waters are open to all countries, which may sail, fly over, fish, lay cables, do research and build artificial islands (Article 87). Each must pay due regard to the others. Building comes with two conditions in the treaty's wording, that the structure be "permitted under international law" and that it respect the continental shelf rules.

Two points in this are often missed. The freedoms are worded as belonging to countries and are not granted to private people, so a person uses them through a country. And no country may validly claim any part of the high seas as its own (Article 89). A new state could not gain a piece of this sea by occupying it, because the rule against claims applies to every state.

The high seas are governed through ships, and each ship carries one country's law with it. A country decides for itself which ships may fly its flag, there must be a genuine link between the country and the ship, and the country must then supervise it (Articles 91 and 94). A ship sails under one flag only and answers to that country on the high seas (Article 92). A warship may not normally board another country's ship. The exceptions are reasonable suspicion of piracy, slave trading, unauthorized broadcasting, having no nationality, or secretly being of the warship's own nationality (Article 110). Having no flag is the main obstacle for a founder, because it lets a warship of any country come aboard to check. The article speaks of ships, so applying it to a fixed structure is an inference and has not been settled.

Suppose a group tows a barge out 300 nautical miles and declares a republic. The first decision is whether to register. Registering with a willing country means accepting that country's law on board. Declaring its own flag means other countries will see no flag at all. Supplies come from a port, which puts the group's boats under that port's law on each visit. The people on board also remain nationals of their home countries, and a country such as the US claims power over certain federal crimes committed by or against its nationals in "any place outside the jurisdiction of any nation" (18 USC 7(7)). Americans still file tax returns under Cook v. Tait, the 1924 Supreme Court case on worldwide income. Giving up US citizenship without holding another nationality leaves a person stateless.

The next question is the seabed, because the water and the sea floor have separate rules. Most of the open ocean is too deep to anchor in cheaply, so a founder would look for a shallow bank. Beyond 200 nautical miles, the sea floor may still be part of a country's extended continental shelf, seabed where that country holds the resource rights (Article 76). The water above stays high seas (Article 78), but artificial islands and fixed structures on that shelf come under the coastal country's control (Articles 60 and 80). Beyond every shelf lies the deep seabed, where no country may claim sovereignty and no person may take any part as their own (Article 137). The International Seabed Authority controls mining there. The treaty does not say plainly whether a long-term mooring on the deep seabed needs anyone's permission, and it gives the owner of the mooring no title to the ground.

A newer treaty adds paperwork for countries that have joined it. The BBNJ Agreement, on marine life in areas outside any country's control, was adopted on 19 June 2023 and took effect on 17 January 2026. In November 2026 it had 145 signing countries and 105 members, and its first members' meeting is set for 11 to 22 January 2027. Members must assess the environmental impact of planned activities under their control there before allowing them (Article 28). The treaty also adds rules on genetic resources from sea life, over which no country may claim authority (Article 11), on marine protected areas, and on helping countries build their capacity.

Then comes money. Published estimates start at about $50 million for a small deep-sea platform and reach billions for a city. Residents would need a bank, and international payments move between banks that hold accounts with each other, called correspondent banks. A place with no banking law and no supervisor gives those banks no one to rely on, so a bank on the platform would have no route to the outside system, and residents would in practice keep accounts in real countries. Selling shares in a future country can count as selling securities, as Lazarus Long found in 1999 when US regulators sued him over $350 million in bonds for a Caribbean nation called New Utopia. He had raised $24,000. Medical care means going ashore. Flag countries must require their captains to help people in danger at sea when they can do so safely (Article 98), and a rescued person is then landed in some other country under its law.

The real cases show where projects stop. Among projects that aimed at the high seas, Aisland is the one where people lived aboard for a long period, and its anchorage in the Persian Gulf was not itself on the high seas. Samuele Landi, an Italian businessman sentenced in his absence to 14 years for fraud, lived on an 800-ton barge about 30 miles off Dubai with shipping containers for quarters. He planned to move to the Saya de Malha Bank, a huge underwater plateau in the Indian Ocean, and hoped for about twenty barges by 2028. On 2 February 2024 a wave broke the barge in two. Landi and two employees died. No government is known to have moved against the barge before that.

The Seasteading Institute, founded in 2008 by Wayne Gramlich and Patri Friedman with $500,000 from Peter Thiel, hoped for a seastead by 2014 and missed the date. It then turned to working inside a country's waters and signed a non-binding memorandum with French Polynesia in 2017. That government pulled out in 2018. Eric Klien's Atlantis Project of 1993, or Oceania, published a full constitution before building anything, needed about $1 billion, and collapsed in April 1994 for lack of interest. Its site, 50 miles off Panama, was in fact inside a coastal resource zone. Anton Bakov, a Russian businessman, failed to buy land from Kiribati and the Gambia and announced Arca Noë in 2020 for what he called neutral Mediterranean waters near Venice. No structure is known to exist.

The commonest misunderstanding is that no owner means no law. In fact every ship, every person aboard and every port call stays attached to some country's law. Another is that a declaration is enough. The tests of statehood in the Montevideo Convention, a 1933 treaty, ask for a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to deal with other countries, and open water gives no territory to define.

The most workable version is a registered vessel under a real flag, with residents agreeing private rules by contract. It would stay under that flag country's law, and it could move if conditions changed. No coastal country holds title here, so the legal position is better than in most places at sea. The rough odds given for this zone, which are judgements and not measurements, are still low for holding out against outside control, because of the cost, the sea itself and the boarding rule, and recognition as a state is put at well under one percent.

eez-shelf.essay:
The sea next to a coast is divided in law into belts, measured outward from a line called the baseline, usually the low-tide edge of the land. A nautical mile, the unit used at sea, is about 1.85 km. The first belt, out to 12 nautical miles, is the territorial sea, where the coastal country has nearly the same authority as on land. The next, reaching 200 nautical miles (about 370 km), is the exclusive economic zone, or EEZ. Under the water lies the continental shelf, the seabed extending out from the coast. In law the shelf reaches at least 200 nautical miles, and in some places it runs further.

These belts come from the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans. Coastal countries wanted the fish, oil and minerals off their shores, and every country wanted ships and aircraft to keep moving. So the coastal country does not own the water outright. It holds rights to the resources (Articles 56 and 57), while others stay free to sail, fly and lay cables, paying due attention to its rights (Article 58). A public road across a farm works in a similar way. Anyone may travel the road, and only the farmer may plant crops or put up a barn. Shelf rights do not depend on occupying the seabed, so a country that has never sent anyone there still holds them (Article 77). The United States has not joined UNCLOS, and it claimed its own 200-mile zone by presidential proclamation in 1983.

A Flanders Marine Institute poster using 2019 data counts 230 EEZs covering 136,850,878 km², leaving out joint arrangements and overlapping claims. It counts each separate zone, so a country with overseas territories appears several times. Russia's single zone is the largest on that count at 7,734,809 km², followed by Australia's at 6,871,622 km². The United States, whose zone is split on the poster among its mainland, Alaska, Hawaii and other areas, has more than 3.4 million square nautical miles in all according to the US agency NOAA, which is about 11.7 million km².

The rule that decides nearly everything is Article 60, which Article 80 extends to the shelf. Only the coastal country may build or authorize three things in its zone. These are artificial islands, installations that have an economic purpose, and any structure that could interfere with its rights. It also has sole legal power over them, including customs, tax, health, safety and immigration law. Artificial islands are not islands in law, so they have no territorial sea of their own and change no sea boundary (Article 60(8)). The country may set safety zones around them, normally of 500 metres at most. It may also board and arrest to enforce its fishing rules (Article 73) and may chase a ship out to sea for violations in the zone, known as hot pursuit (Article 111).

Suppose a group anchors a platform 100 miles off Florida and declares it independent. The spot is inside the US EEZ, so the first question is whether the structure had US permission. If the group asks and gets it, the platform comes under US tax and immigration law, and the independence it wanted is gone. If it does not ask, the record offers comparisons. In the 1960s promoters began building on Triumph and Long Reefs, about four and a half miles off Florida and outside the narrow belt the US then claimed. In 1970, in United States v. Ray, a US appeals court ordered a permanent ban, holding that the country's exclusive rights over its shelf were enough even though it did not own the reefs. When a company proposed a nation called Taluga on Cortes Bank, about 111 miles off San Diego, the US government reportedly declared the bank US territory as part of its shelf. That wording goes further than shelf law, which gives rights over the seabed and its resources and does not make the seabed part of the country.

One part of the law is unclear. UNCLOS does not define "artificial island", and it does not say whether a small floating home on a mooring is an island, an installation or a ship. The answer matters. An artificial island falls under the coastal country whatever it is used for. An installation falls under it only if it has an economic purpose or could interfere with the country's rights. A boat passing through is plainly using the freedom to sail. A structure that stays put and houses people for the long term looks more like what Article 60 covers, which appears to rule out an independent project unless the coastal country agrees. The coastal country has the boats on site, so its reading takes effect first and any court comes later.

The clearest real case is XLII, a six-metre-wide cabin on a weighted column in the Andaman Sea, built by a company called Ocean Builders. Its owners said it sat just over 12 nautical miles off Phuket, and other accounts say about 14. The American bitcoin trader Chad Elwartowski and his Thai partner Supranee Thepdet moved in during early 2019, and he said 20 more would be sold. The Thai navy said they had announced autonomy beyond the reach of any court. The couple left before the navy raided the cabin on 13 April. Thailand revoked his visa and charged them under a law carrying life in prison or death, saying they had endangered national sovereignty, and navy boats towed the cabin toward shore as evidence. Ocean Builders argued that the site was in the contiguous zone, the band 12 to 24 miles out where a country has limited powers, and that no micronation was intended. Thailand pointed to its EEZ. In July prosecutors said nine more suspects would be charged. How the case ended is not known, so no court is known to have decided whether Thailand's criminal law reached that far.

A real country gets no special treatment under these rules. In 2011 President Anote Tong of Kiribati, whose low-lying islands are threatened by rising seas, said his government was considering floating islands, at about $2 billion to come from other countries. He named no site, three years later his government bought land in Fiji, and no platform was built. A platform would not by itself carry the sea rights that natural land generates.

If the structure counts as a ship, it needs a real country's flag, which brings that country's law on board (Articles 91 and 94). Ocean Builders' later cruise ship plan, the MS Satoshi, collapsed in 2020 because no insurer would provide the liability cover a ship's owners need. Payments between countries travel through banks that hold accounts with each other, and those banks need a supervisor they can rely on, which a platform lacks. One law journal puts a small deep-sea platform for a few residents at $50 million, and selling stakes to raise such money can count as selling investments. The US regulator sued the promoter of New Utopia over a $350 million bond offering that raised $24,000.

Tax follows the person. The US taxes citizens on worldwide income wherever they live, as the Supreme Court held in Cook v. Tait in 1924. Food, fuel and parts come through a port, and that port's country sets the terms. Ship captains are required to help people in danger at sea when they safely can (Article 98), and a rescued person lands in some other country under its law, so serious medical care means going ashore. A birth, marriage or will on a platform would need a registry others accept, and without one a child's papers and an inheritance would appear to depend on the parents' home countries.

The commonest misunderstanding is that everything past 12 nautical miles is international waters. That is correct for passing ships and aircraft and wrong for resources and fixed structures. A second is that a declaration changes the zone. The usual test for a state, in the Montevideo Convention of 1933, asks for a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to deal with other countries, and a structure that is no island in law provides no territory.

The most workable version is an agreement with the coastal country, which alone can authorize the structure and could write special rules for it into its own law. Such grants have proved fragile, on land and at sea. Honduras changed its constitution in 2013 to allow private zones such as Próspera, on an island, and its Supreme Court struck those laws down in 2024. French Polynesia signed a memorandum with the Seasteading Institute in 2017 and said in 2018 that it was void. Whatever freedom exists is a grant from one government that a later government can review.

territorial-sea.essay:
The territorial sea is the belt of water next to a coast. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, a country may set it at up to 12 nautical miles (about 22 km) from its baselines, the lines from which sea zones are measured (Article 3). The normal baseline is the low-water line on the country's official charts (Article 5).

Inside this belt the coastal country has full authority over the water, the seabed under it and the air above it, the same as over its land (Article 2). The main limit is innocent passage, the right of foreign ships to pass through peacefully and without delay (Articles 17 to 19). A private road that the owner must let travellers use is similar, since a traveller may drive through and may not stop and build a house. Passage has to be continuous, and stopping is allowed only for ordinary navigation, emergencies or helping people in danger (Article 18), so settling in one spot falls outside it.

A further belt, the contiguous zone, can reach out to 24 nautical miles if the country declares one. There the country may act to prevent or punish customs, tax, immigration and health offences committed in its territory or territorial sea (Article 33).

The practical result is that a structure here is a domestic building project. Suppose a group anchors a platform 5 nautical miles off a coast and declares independence. The group is inside the country, in the same legal position as someone who puts up an unapproved building on land and announces that it is a new state. Harbour, building, tax and police officials all have ordinary powers. A nearby officer can visit, and the group's boats have to land at that country's docks.

Giorgio Rosa's Rose Island shows how little room there is even near the line. His 400-square-metre platform stood nearly 12 km off Rimini, a few hundred metres outside Italian waters as they were then measured. The Rimini harbour office asked him to stop in late 1966. He declared independence on 1 May 1968, and police and tax officers took control on 26 June, 56 days later. A project inside the limit would not even have the argument about position that Rosa made.

The line itself is less simple than it looks, and two British cases teach this. Roy Bates ran a pirate radio station on Knock John, a wartime fort about 16 km off Essex, where British broadcasting law could reach him only if the fort lay inside the three-mile limit then used. Distance is measured from a line set by law, which need not follow the shore. Magistrates fined him £100 in 1966, and his appeal failed when the court held that the fort lay on the landward side of that line. Radio 390, on Red Sands fort, lost in the High Court in December 1966, two judges to one, because the distance could be measured from a sandbank that shows only at low water. UNCLOS keeps the same idea today. Land that shows only at low tide can serve as a baseline if it lies within the territorial sea's width of the coast (Article 13). Neither fort had moved. A person therefore cannot judge the limit with a map and a ruler from the beach.

A country can also move the line. Bates went on to Roughs Tower, which he declared to be Sealand in 1967. The fort sits about 6 to 7 nautical miles off the English coast, or about 11 to 13 km, and at that time it was outside British waters. A British court said so in 1968, when it held that it could not try his son on firearms charges there. In 1987 the UK extended its territorial waters to 12 nautical miles, which put the fort in waters recognized as British. Offshore installations and artificial islands, for their part, do not count as harbour works and cannot push the boundary out in the builder's favour (Article 11). So the limit can grow toward a project, and a project cannot grow the limit.

Three real projects show what is possible when the country's law is accepted from the start. The Seasteading Institute of San Francisco chose French Polynesia, a self-governing French territory, for its calm lagoons. In January 2017 the territory's government signed a memorandum of understanding with the institute, a document that records intentions and is usually weaker than a contract. It opened the way to studies of "seazones" with a special governing framework, and the institute formed a company, Blue Frontiers. Residents objected and opposition politician Valentina Cross protested. On 28 February 2018 it was reported that the government considered the deal to have no legal force and to have expired at the end of 2017. Nothing was built. The memorandum had bound the government to very little, so it could simply let the plan lapse.

SeaPods came from Ocean Builders, the same company whose cabin off Phuket was raided by the Thai navy in 2019. It turned to homes at Linton Bay Marina in Panama, with $100 deposits and prices from about $295,000 to $1.5 million. Each home stands above the water on a float tethered to the seabed by anchors. At the unveiling on 22 September 2022, in front of an audience that included Panama's president, the prototype tipped over with people inside. The company blamed a failed bilge pump, the pump that clears water from a hull, and denied that it sank, and no injuries were reported. Guests were staying in one by June 2023. The company claims no independence, and the number of permanent residents is not known.

Oceanix Busan is the largest of the three. On 18 November 2021 the city of Busan in South Korea, UN-Habitat and the company OCEANIX agreed to build a prototype floating district, with about $200 million anticipated as the cost, and they unveiled the design at UN Headquarters in April 2022. At the developers' later figure of $10,000 per square metre, its 15.5 acres would come to about $627 million. A conference in October 2023 gave no concrete financing or construction plans, construction is not known to have started, and no one is known to live there. This project attempts to build on the sea while staying fully inside South Korean law.

The ordinary bumps follow from being inside a country. Permits come first, and residents can stop them, as in French Polynesia. Ocean Builders' cruise ship plan outside national waters collapsed in 2020 when no insurer would give liability cover, which shows how much depends on insurance anywhere at sea. Tax on residents stays as it was. The US taxes citizens on worldwide income, and the host country may tax local income too. Medical care, schooling, inheritance and birth records run through the country's normal systems, which is an advantage for families. Police and courts have the same reach as on the shore, so a dispute over a floating home would go to an ordinary local court.

The common misunderstandings come from treating water as different from land. A boat's flag does not take a settled home out of the coastal country's law, since passage rights do not cover staying. A declaration does not change the zone either. Stuart Hill, who declared a Shetland islet the state of Forvik in 2008, was still charged with motoring offences in a Scottish court. Recognition is as far away as it is anywhere else, since UN membership needs nine of 15 Security Council votes with no veto and two-thirds of the General Assembly.

The most workable version is a licensed floating neighbourhood or marina, or at most a special zone written into the host country's law by its legislature. Calm water, short supply lines and a nearby hospital make building here among the easier options at sea, and holding out against the coastal country close to impossible. Any self-government lasts only as long as that country's politics allow, and a memorandum alone gives no protection.

reefs-low-tide-elevations.essay:
A reef is shallow and often far from any town, so founders have often chosen one as a place to start a country. The law treats it according to two facts, whether the feature stays dry at high tide and which legal zone of the sea it lies in.

The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, sorts features by what the sea does to them. An island is naturally formed land, surrounded by water and above water at high tide. A rock is an island that cannot support human habitation or an economic life of its own. It gets a territorial sea, a belt of coastal water of up to 12 nautical miles (about 22 km), and no exclusive economic zone or continental shelf, the wider belts of resource and seabed rights (Articles 3 and 121). A low-tide elevation is natural land that is above water only at low tide. More than 12 nautical miles from land, it has no territorial sea of its own (Article 13). A bank that stays under water at all times, such as Cortes Bank or the Saya de Malha Bank, is simply part of the seabed. Many of the reefs and banks that founders have chosen fall into these last two groups.

In 2016 a panel of judges set up under UNCLOS, in a case the Philippines brought against China over the South China Sea, ruled on this. It found that Mischief Reef, Second Thomas Shoal and Subi Reef are low-tide elevations and "not features that are capable of appropriation by occupation or otherwise". It also held that a feature's status depends on its natural condition, before any building. It found that no feature in the Spratly Islands can generate an exclusive economic zone, and that they cannot do so collectively as a unit. China took no part in the case and rejects the ruling, which formally binds only those two countries. On the panel's reasoning, a low-tide reef cannot be claimed by moving onto it, and it belongs to whichever legal zone it lies in.

That reasoning closes the most natural idea, which is to dump sand until the reef stays dry. Filling in a reef makes an artificial island, and an artificial island generates no territorial sea (Article 60(8)). Building is physically possible, as Minerva's founders showed in 1971 by barging sand from Australia. If the reef is inside a country's exclusive economic zone, the belt up to 200 nautical miles from its coast, that country must authorize the work and sets any safety zone around it (Article 60).

Suppose a group finds a reef 100 nautical miles from a country's coast and starts to build. The first question is whose zone it is in, and a reef that far out normally answers to that country. United States v. Ray shows what happens next. In the 1960s two rival groups, the Grand Capri Republic and Atlantis, Isle of Gold, planned countries on Triumph and Long Reefs, about four and a half miles off southeast Florida, in what were then international waters. The US Army Corps of Engineers refused a permit in 1964, and Louis Ray dredged anyway. A trial court barred building in 1969 and rejected a trespass claim, since the government did not own the reefs. In 1970 the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit held that the reefs were part of the outer continental shelf, where US law and the Geneva Convention on the Continental Shelf give the country exclusive rights to resources, and it ordered a full permanent ban, noting harm to corals and shipping.

The Republic of Minerva shows the other route, which is annexation, meaning a country formally adding the place to its territory. Michael Oliver, a Nevada real estate developer, raised money from about 2,000 investors, and his group declared independence on the reefs between Fiji and Tonga on 19 January 1972. Tonga had not included them in its 1887 claim. At a conference on 24 February 1972, about five weeks later, Australia, New Zealand, Fiji, Nauru, Samoa and the Cook Islands backed a Tongan claim. Tonga proclaimed the reefs and the waters within 12 miles on 15 June, and an expedition arrived on 18 June. The king came with a convict work party, and the platform was dismantled within hours. In 1982 a group led by Morris Davis, Minerva's former provisional president, tried again, and Tongan troops forced them off after three weeks. Annexing the reef then left two states arguing. Fiji rejected Tonga's sea claims from the reefs in 2005, its navy destroyed navigation equipment there in 2010 and 2011, and the dispute is not known to have been settled. How the 2016 reasoning would apply to Tonga's older claim has not been tested in court.

Other projects ended earlier. Operation Atlantis, begun by the soap executive Werner Stiefel in 1968, lost a concrete boat to capsizing and then to a storm. At Silver Shoals, described in accounts of the project as claimed by both Haiti and the Bahamas, gunboats ordered his group away, and accounts differ on whose they were. Haiti cancelled a lease on Tortuga after officials read the group's newsletter, and a hurricane destroyed an oil rig bound for the Misteriosa Bank. Abalonia, planned in 1966 for Cortes Bank about 111 miles off San Diego, lost its anchor ship when waves broke it up on Bishop Rock. A later plan there, Taluga, was stopped when the US declared the bank part of its continental shelf. Leicester Hemingway's raft New Atlantis, 8 by 30 feet off Jamaica, relied on the US Guano Islands Act of 1856, was refused by the Universal Postal Union when it tried to sell stamps, and was destroyed by storms before any court tested it. Autopia, on the Saya de Malha Bank in the Indian Ocean, stalled for lack of money after a steel frame was built in 2002. Its founders called the site high seas. Most of the bank does lie in international waters, but part lies in the exclusive economic zone of Mauritius, which treats the bank as under its administration, so the position depends on the exact spot.

Money brings its own legal risk. New Utopia, planned for the Misteriosa Bank, was never built and existed as an offer of bonds at 9.5 percent. On 8 April 1999 the US Securities and Exchange Commission sued, a judge froze the money, and in January 2000 Lazarus Long, the promoter, accepted a final judgment. The SEC says about $24,000 was raised. Investors, insurers and banks all live in real countries, so their rules reach the project wherever its reef is.

Then come the physical problems. A low-tide reef has no fresh water and no soil, and storms have destroyed rafts, ships and rigs in the cases above. A reef also carries environmental duties. The South China Sea panel held that building land at seven reefs breached a country's duties on the marine environment. Serious medical care means a boat to someone else's port, and people there remain under their home countries' law, including US tax on worldwide income.

Two misunderstandings recur. One is that "international waters" means no one can stop a project. The shelf rules defeated this idea at Grand Capri and Cortes Bank. Another is that a reef beyond every country's zone would be free for the taking. The seabed there belongs to the deep ocean floor regime under UNCLOS, and no country or person may take any part of it as their own (Article 137). A declaration of independence also does not supply the "defined territory" that the Montevideo Convention, the 1933 treaty defining a state, requires.

The most workable version is modest. A coastal country can license a research or reef restoration station on a reef in its zone, and the station then operates under that country's law. Another version is to give up the reef altogether. A participant in Operation Atlantis says the group later bought Hatchet Caye, an ordinary island in Belize, and lived there until 2005. A reef can offer a physical base for a while. It offers little legal protection, and nearby states have repeatedly acted within months.

abandoned-platforms.essay:
Steel and concrete structures stand in open water off many coasts, and some are no longer in use. A disused platform already has a deck and legs and needs no dredging, so people have tried since the 1960s to use wartime sea forts and purpose-built platforms as bases for independent projects.

The first thing to understand is that an empty structure is not an ownerless one. Two separate kinds of right apply. One is ownership, which belongs to whichever company or government built or bought it, and entering without permission can be trespass. The other is legal power over the place, which belongs to a country. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, an installation in a country's exclusive economic zone, the belt of sea up to 200 nautical miles from its coast where it controls resources, stays under that country's sole legal power. The same applies on its continental shelf, the seabed extending out from the coast (Articles 60 and 80). Oil platforms stand on a shelf, so they normally fall under that power. Buying a platform from its owner would appear to transfer ownership only, because the country's legal power does not come with the sale.

The treaty also expects old structures to disappear. Abandoned or disused installations must be removed to keep shipping safe, and any part left standing must be made public so that ships can avoid it (Article 60(3)). In practice that duty usually reaches the operator through the coastal country's own rules. Sinking one is no easy way out, since the London Protocol, a treaty on dumping, treats all dumping at sea as prohibited unless explicitly permitted. A platform has no territorial sea, the belt of coastal water that land has, so it cannot be the base of a claim to the water around it (Article 60(8)). Nor is it part of the coast when boundaries are drawn (Article 11).

Suppose a group boards a disused oil platform 50 miles off a coast and raises a flag. Boarding is physically possible. The owner, who may still be responsible for removing the platform, now has unauthorized people on its property. The coastal country has legal power over the structure, so its police or navy can come out. If anyone is hurt, or the structure fails, the questions of who pays would go to that country's courts.

Sealand is the case everyone cites. Roughs Tower was built by Britain in 1943 and sunk in place on a sandbar, about 6 nautical miles off Suffolk and 7 off Essex. That was then outside Britain's three-mile territorial sea. Roy Bates, a former army major, had just lost a court case over Radio Essex on Knock John, another fort, because the court found that fort lay on the landward side of the legal line measuring the limit. He moved to Roughs Tower, took it from Radio Caroline staff, and declared the Principality of Sealand on 2 September 1967. In May 1968 his son Michael fired a pistol near a boat servicing a buoy. A judge at Chelmsford ruled that October that the firearms law did not apply, because Parliament had never extended it beyond three miles. That ruling decided only how far a statute reached. In 1978 a Cologne court held that Sealand was no state, in a case brought by Alexander Achenbach, a German who had drafted its constitution. That August Achenbach's associates seized the fort while the elder Bateses were away, and the family retook it by helicopter. In 1987 Britain extended its territorial sea to 12 miles, which now covers the tower, and it has left the place alone since. The Bates family says Britain and Germany have recognized it in practice, and neither government accepts this. Roy Bates died in 2012. Michael lives in England, the family sells titles and an online citizenship at about $10 a month, and one caretaker lives on the fort. Sealand's fort stood outside the limit when the claim began, and a new project would not have that history.

Other governments did not leave their forts alone. Sunk Head, about 18 km off Essex, stood clearly outside British waters too. When the law banning offshore broadcasting took effect in August 1967, Royal Engineers placed 3,200 pounds of explosives and blew it up on 21 August, leaving only stumps. Red Sands, home of Radio 390, lost in the High Court in 1966 on a measurement from a sandbank that shows only at low water, and it went off the air on 14 August 1967 under the Marine Broadcasting Offences Act. In June 1966 men boarded Radio City's fort in a dispute over a transmitter, its owner Reginald Calvert was shot dead at the home of a rival, Oliver Smedley, and Smedley was cleared on grounds of self-defence. The killing turned public feeling against the stations, and enforcement rose.

REM Island was built for commercial radio and television about 10 km off Noordwijk and fixed to the seabed in cement, beyond Dutch territorial waters as then measured. Broadcasts began in August 1964. On 12 December the Dutch government passed a law dividing up the North Sea floor, under which the seabed below the platform counted as Dutch, and marines boarded five days later. Rose Island, a 400-square-metre platform nearly 12 km off Rimini, declared independence on 1 May 1968. Italian police and tax officers took control on 26 June, 56 days later, and blockaded it. The navy set explosive charges twice in February 1969, the second time on 13 February, and a storm sank what remained on 26 February. The Council of State, Italy's top administrative court, held the independence claims unfounded and said Italian citizens stay subject to Italian law abroad.

Holding a fort leaves the other problems open. HavenCo was set up on Sealand in 2000 to keep customers' data beyond the reach of courts. Law professor James Grimmelmann found that the dot-com crash cut Sealand's internet links more than any government did. Co-founder Ryan Lackey left in 2002 after disputes with the Bates family and could not sue, because Sealand's monarch headed its courts and going to a foreign court would have undercut the claim of independence. Operations stopped in 2008. Banks need a supervisor they can rely on, and a fort has none. Sealand's passports were revoked in 1997 after a Madrid-based ring sold fakes, and using such a document at a border may bring charges. Unauthorized broadcasting from the high seas can be prosecuted by several countries, including any country that receives the signal, and their ships may arrest those involved (Article 109). Old steel and concrete need upkeep, and a 2006 fire on Sealand sent one person to hospital, with damage estimates ranging from £100,000 to half a million pounds. People on board keep their home countries' tax duties, and a rescue lands them in another country. Locking someone up on the platform could also be treated as unlawful detention by another country's courts, since no one else accepts the platform's own courts.

Common misunderstandings follow from Sealand's fame. The 1968 British ruling said a statute stopped at three miles and did not recognize Sealand. Occupying a structure gives no title to it, and buying one gives no country. The usual test for a state, in the Montevideo Convention of 1933, asks for a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to deal with others. Sealand has had one or two residents in recent years, and its territory is a deck that UNCLOS treats as no island.

The most workable version is an ordinary lease or purchase from the owner, with the coastal country's approval, for a business such as research or tourism, under that country's law and with a plan for eventual removal. REM Island's later life points the same way. The Dutch government used it to measure sea temperature and salt levels, and it has been a restaurant in Amsterdam's harbour since 2011. A new occupation claiming independence would have little legal basis on a shelf or in an exclusive economic zone, and most of its chance of lasting would depend on a government choosing not to act.

disputed-islands.essay:
A disputed island is land that more than one country says is its own. The best-known examples are the Spratly and Paracel Islands in the South China Sea. China, Taiwan and Vietnam each claim both groups. The Philippines and Malaysia claim parts of the Spratlys, and Brunei claims a zone reaching into them. A place with several rival owners can look as if it has no owner, but each claimant holds that the land is already its own, and they keep armed garrisons there. A newcomer would be one more claimant facing armed occupiers.

The natural land is small. The Spratlys' naturally formed islands come to about 177 hectares, less than 2 square kilometres, spread over a large area of sea. Building has since added far more than that. The US Defense Department reported in 2016 that China alone had reclaimed about 3,200 acres, or about 1,300 hectares, in the South China Sea, and Vietnam has also been enlarging its outposts. The Paracels are more than 30 islands, under Chinese control in practice since 1974. The value lies mostly in the water and seabed around them, because under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, land can generate rights over nearby sea.

Those rights depend on what kind of land it is. A true island gets the full set, including an exclusive economic zone, the belt up to 200 nautical miles where a country controls resources, and a continental shelf, meaning seabed rights. Rocks that cannot support human habitation or an economic life of their own get neither of those (Article 121). In 2016 a tribunal, a panel of judges set up under UNCLOS, decided a case brought by the Philippines against China. Its award of 12 July 2016 found that no feature in the Spratlys can generate an exclusive economic zone, individually or as a group. It found no legal basis for China to claim historic rights to resources inside the nine-dash line, the line China uses for its claims in the sea. It also found that China's land-building at seven features caused severe harm to coral and violated its duties, and that China built on Mischief Reef inside the Philippines' exclusive economic zone. Under the treaty the award is final and binding on those two countries (Article 296). China took no part, says the award is void and does not follow it.

The tribunal ruled on sea zones and said it does not rule on any question of who holds authority over land territory. Who owns each island remains a matter between the claimant countries. Land-building creates no new territorial sea, the belt of coastal water that natural land has (Article 60(8)), and because the tribunal held that a feature's legal status depends on its natural condition, engineering work gains no legal ground on that reasoning.

Two older rulings show how such disputes between countries have been decided. In the Island of Palmas case of 1928, the arbitrator Max Huber held that discovery gives only a starting claim, that being nearby gives nothing, and that continuous and peaceful display of the functions of a state is as good as a title. In the Clipperton case of 1931, the arbitrator found that on an uninhabited island a state's clear intention and brief presence can be enough. Both rulings concern states competing with states, and the acts they describe are acts of government.

Suppose a group lands on an unoccupied sandbar in the Spratlys and raises its own flag. The first response would likely come from whichever country holds the nearest feature, and removing the group would need no court. No one is known to have tried this recently, so the best guide is what happened to earlier claimants.

Tomás Cloma was a Filipino businessman with a fishing fleet and a maritime school. On 11 May 1956 his brother Filemon led 40 men in taking formal possession of 53 islands and islets some 380 miles west of Palawan, and they posted a Notice to the Whole World. Tomás argued the area had no owner because Japan had given it up in the 1951 San Francisco peace treaty, and he declared the Free Territory of Freedomland on 21 May. In October 1956 Taiwanese naval ships met Filemon's boat at North Danger Reef, and Taiwan later burned buildings and took property. The brothers then asked the Philippine government for support. In 1972 President Marcos jailed Tomás for four months for impersonating an officer by using the title admiral. In December 1974 he was arrested and made to sign over his rights to the Philippines for one peso, and a 1978 decree made the area the Municipality of Kalayaan. The Philippines cites that transfer as one basis for its own title. So the private claim survived only as an asset of a state.

An older rival was the Republic of Morac-Songhrati-Meads, a claim made only in documents. Its supporters said a British captain, James George Meads, claimed the islands in 1877, and none of this has been shown to be true. The first checkable evidence comes from 1946, when Morton F. Meads, an American soldier, was discharged in Manila. His stories drew Cloma's attention. The group never set up a settlement, its requests for recognition in 1972 went nowhere, and its $25 billion lawsuit of 1985 was never heard.

In 1893 James Harden-Hickey proclaimed himself Prince of Trindade, an uninhabited South Atlantic island, and sold bonds. Britain took possession in 1895 for a telegraph station, Brazil won the dispute with Britain, and the Brazilian navy keeps a post there. The Kingdom of EnenKio claimed Wake Island, controlled by the United States since 1899 and also claimed by the Marshall Islands. The Marshall Islands government condemned it in 1998, and in October 2000 the US Securities and Exchange Commission won a court order freezing the assets of Robert Moore over $1 billion of unregistered Gold War Bonds. How that case ended is not known.

Rockall, a bare rock in the North Atlantic, shows a gentler response. Britain claimed it in 1955 and made it part of Scotland in 1972, and Ireland, Iceland and Denmark have contested the rights around it. Greenpeace landed in June 1997 to protest oil exploration, stayed 42 days and declared the Global State of Waveland. The British government answered that Rockall was British and that anyone was free to go there and stay as long as they pleased, which treated the activists as ordinary visitors. Tom McClean had earlier spent 40 days there in 1985 to strengthen the British claim, and Nick Hancock reached 45 days alone in 2014. These stays did not change the rock's legal class. Britain joined UNCLOS in 1997, and it has since said that Rockall gets a 12-mile territorial sea and no economic zone or shelf of its own.

Everyday problems come after the military one. Supplies would come by boat from a port belonging to a claimant or a neighbour, and a serious injury would mean rescue into one of those countries. Building would raise the coral damage the tribunal condemned. A passport or stamp from such a place gets no recognition, and UN membership needs nine of 15 Security Council votes with no veto, on a council where China holds a permanent seat.

The most common misunderstanding is that a dispute creates a gap, when to each claimant a newcomer is an intruder on its own territory. Another is that a court win for one country, such as the 2016 award, opens the islands to others. It decided sea rights only.

A private person can realistically do two things here. One is to visit or work under the administration of whichever claimant holds a feature, accepting that country's rules and the risk that its rivals object. The other is a short protest occupation in the style of Waveland, whose value is publicity and which has no standing in any country's law. States with existing claims have little reason to accept a new one.

moon.essay:
The Moon is the natural body that circles Earth, about 385,000 kilometres away, with a radius of about 1,740 kilometres. Its gravity is one-sixth of Earth's, and its very thin atmosphere gives no protection from the Sun's radiation or from falling rocks. The ground reaches about 127 C in full sun and falls to about -173 C in darkness. Ice lies in permanently shadowed craters near the poles. It is the only other world people have walked on, although no one has stayed longer than a few days, so the legal questions are closest to being tested here.

The basic rules come from the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main treaty on what countries may do in space. Everyone has free access to all areas (Article I). No country may take over the Moon by claiming authority over it, by using or occupying it, or by any other means (Article II). The Moon may be used for peaceful purposes only, with no military bases, weapons tests or military exercises (Article IV). Private activity needs permission and continuing oversight from a treaty country, which answers for it (Article VI).

The treaty also separates things from ground. An object that a country has registered stays the property of its owner, and the registering country keeps legal power over the object and its staff, on the surface as well (Article VIII). Countries must avoid harmful contamination and pay due attention to the interests of others (Article IX). Stations are open to visits by representatives of other members, on a reciprocal basis and with advance notice (Article XII).

The result resembles a tent on a public campsite, where the tent is yours and the ground never becomes yours. The Soviet probe Luna 2 scattered metal pennants marked "USSR" when it crashed in 1959, and they gave no claim. The descent stage and flag of Apollo 11, and the rover of Apollo 17, remain American property on ground that is not American. The same holds for China's Chang'e 4 and Chang'e 6, India's Vikram lander at the place India calls Shiv Shakti point, and Japan's silent SLIM lander. The wreck of Russia's Luna 25 is still Russian property. Firefly's Blue Ghost lander belongs to a private company, and the United States still answers for it.

A second treaty, the Moon Agreement, took effect in July 1984 after Austria became the fifth country to join. It calls the Moon the "common heritage of mankind", meaning it belongs to humanity as a whole, and says its surface cannot become the property of any country, organization or person (Article 11). A future set of rules is to govern commercial use of its resources, and those rules have never been written. Countries may build stations using only the area they need, and they must tell the UN (Article 9). As of 1 January 2026 it had 17 members and 4 countries that signed without joining, and no leading space power is a member. American campaigners fought it in 1979 and 1980, and the United States stayed out. Saudi Arabia left with effect from 5 January 2024. A country that has not joined is not bound by it.

The newer approach is the Artemis Accords, a US-led set of principles first signed by eight countries in October 2020. They describe themselves as a political commitment and not a treaty, so they create no duty that a court could enforce. NASA counts 78 signers, the latest Vietnam on 28 October 2026. China and Russia are not among them. The Accords say that extracting resources does not in itself count as a country taking over the body (Section 10). They also create "safety zones", areas where signers give notice of their work and coordinate to avoid interference, with a size that follows the work done there and an end when the work stops (Section 11). NASA says this respects free access. It is the most debated part of the Accords, because critics fear that a zone others must keep clear of could work in practice like a claim, and no court has tested it. A US law, 51 USC 51303, lets American citizens own and sell space resources they recover, subject to the country's international obligations. China and Russia lead a rival project, the International Lunar Research Station, with construction planned from 2031. Both camps want the area around Shackleton crater at the south pole because of its ice, and the Outer Space Treaty bars either from claiming it.

Private deeds sit apart from all this. A. Dean Lindsay of Georgia claimed space objects before a notary in the 1930s, and Robert Coles later sold Moon lots at a dollar an acre. James Mangan's Nation of Celestial Space claimed all of space in 1949 and applied to join the UN. Jenaro Gajardo Vera, a Chilean lawyer, declared himself owner of the Moon in 1954, partly to meet a social club's rule that members own property. The property registry has no record of the deed. Dennis Hope filed a claim in 1980, told the UN, treats its silence as approval, and sells deeds through his Lunar Embassy. Discover magazine reported 4.25 million buyers and over $9 million in sales. The Official Lunar Registry charges about $20 an acre. Virgiliu Pop, a Romanian space lawyer, traced these claims in his book Unreal Estate and took apart Hope's legal argument. The International Institute of Space Law, a professional body of space lawyers, warned that such deeds raise the chance that individuals will be misled. No government or court is known to back one, and a buyer receives a printed paper.

Suppose a group wants its own settlement. The first bump is permission. In the United States a launch needs a licence from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), with insurance for harm to others of up to $500 million. Radio frequencies are assigned through the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), a UN agency, and only member countries can file. The Moon Express case shows how unformed this still is. In 2016 no US agency was clearly in charge of a private landing, so the company asked the FAA, which issued a favourable review. Lawyers at the group TechFreedom doubted that one letter met the treaty's demand for continuing oversight, and the mission never flew. Lonestar's small data centre, marketed as beyond national data rules, reached the Moon on the Athena lander in 2025. The lander fell on its side, the mission ended in about 13 hours, and the United States answers for that hardware too.

Money comes next. A Falcon 9 rocket costs about $3,246 per kilogram to low orbit, and the Moon is much farther. Food at 2.77 kilograms a day comes to about 1,000 kilograms a person each year, which would be about $3.3 million even at the low-orbit rate. The International Space Station costs about $3 billion a year to run.

On site, no one can lawfully keep others out, because access is free to all, though safety zones may limit access in practice. For All Moonkind, a nonprofit, helped pass a US law in 2020 protecting old landing sites, which binds only companies working with NASA, and the Accords commit signers to preserve such sites (Section 9). In an emergency, astronauts of member countries must help each other (Article V), and specialist care means going home. Crime stays under outside law, since the registering country has power over the base and US law reaches offences by or against US nationals outside any nation. American settlers would still owe US tax returns, under a 1924 Supreme Court case, Cook v. Tait.

Declaring independence would change little. The usual test of statehood, from the Montevideo Convention of 1933, requires a defined territory, and the ban on national claims leaves no land on the Moon for a new state to hold. UN membership requires a Security Council recommendation and two-thirds of the General Assembly.

The most workable version is a licensed base under a cooperating country, with residents' own rules made by contract and with a safety zone announced around the work. The rough odds given for this zone, which are judgements and not measurements, put building even that at about 5 percent. Whoever arrives first with a state's support gains practical influence over a site, which lasts only as long as the work and carries no title. Residents stay subject to the licensing country.

leo.essay:
Low Earth orbit is the band of space closest to the planet, under 2,000 km up according to the European Space Agency. The International Space Station (ISS) and China's Tiangong station circle there, along with most satellites. Because it can be reached with rockets that are already for sale, and because no country owns it, this is the first place in space that people imagine settling. The law here was written for governments, long before any private station.

During the Cold War, governments worried that a rival might claim the Moon or put weapons in orbit, and in 1967 they wrote the Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on what countries may do in space. It had 118 member countries and 23 that had signed without joining as at 1 January 2026, up from 116 a year earlier with the addition of Latvia and Malaysia. Space is free for all countries to use (Article I), and no country may take it over by claiming authority, by using or occupying it, or by any other means (Article II). Read alone, those two articles look like an opening for founders.

The next articles take that opening away. Countries answer for private space activities, which need permission and continuing oversight from an appropriate member country (Article VI). A launching country is legally bound to pay for damage (Article VII). The country that registers an object keeps legal power and control over it and anyone on board (Article VIII). Countries must also pay due attention to others and consult before causing harmful interference (Article IX). So nobody can own the place, and every object in it falls under the legal system of some country on Earth, much as every ship on the high seas has a flag state.

Three more treaties fill in the details. The Registration Convention, with 77 members, requires the launching country to list each object in a register and report its details to the UN. Only launching countries and qualifying international organizations run such registers, so a private person appears to have no way to register alone. The Liability Convention, with 100 members plus 4 organizations that accept it by declaration, makes a launching country pay for damage on Earth or to aircraft whether or not it was at fault. Elsewhere in space it pays only if it was at fault. The Rescue Agreement, on helping astronauts in distress, has 100 members plus 3 declarations. A country that can be billed for what its citizens launch has a reason to license them.

Suppose a group wants an independent orbital station. The first obstacle is on the ground, because no one can leave Earth without a launching country. That country must give permission, register the station and keep legal power over it. A US citizen or US company launching from anywhere outside the US still needs a licence from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the US aviation regulator (51 USC 50904). The licence requires insurance for harm to others, capped at $500 million or the most available at reasonable cost, and the government can block a launch on safety, national security or foreign policy grounds. People on board must be told in writing that the government has not certified the vehicle, and US rules on occupant safety are largely on hold in a learning period set to end on January 1, 2028. A group would buy its launch from a licensed operator, under that licensing system.

The second step is radio. A station must talk to the ground, and radio contact needs a filing with the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the UN agency for radio coordination, through a member country. The ITU's founding treaty treats orbits and frequencies as limited natural resources and forbids harmful interference (ITU Constitution, Articles 44 and 45). Swarm Technologies shows that this reaches past borders. The US regulator, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), refused in December 2017 to license its four tiny satellites, fearing they could not be tracked. Swarm launched them anyway on 12 January 2018 on an Indian rocket. It paid a $900,000 penalty and accepted a compliance plan. The foreign launch made no difference, because the company was American and its satellites signalled ground stations in Georgia. In 2023 the FCC also fined Dish Network $150,000 for leaving a satellite, in a much higher orbit, too low at the end of its life.

Flags of convenience, the practice of registering a ship in a country with light rules, have been proposed for space. The limit is that a country whose soil was used for the launch stays liable, whichever country keeps the register. No court has tested this.

Asgardia shows what a declaration achieves. Igor Ashurbeyli announced this self-declared space nation in 2016. On 12 November 2017 an Antares rocket from Virginia carried its 2.8 kg satellite, Asgardia-1, to orbit on a NASA-funded mission flown by US companies, and legal scholars pointed out that it stayed under US authority. It burned up on 12 September 2022 with no replacement known. No one has ever lived there, and no state or UN body recognises it.

Money and supplies come next. The ISS costs about $3 billion a year to operate, according to NASA's Inspector General, and its crews still rely on delivered tanks, water and food. At about $3,246 per kg on a Falcon 9 rocket, food at 2.77 kg a day comes to about $3.3 million per person each year in launch costs alone. MirCorp, which leased the Russian station Mir and paid for its last crew in 2000, ran out of money and lost Mir when it was brought down in March 2001. Bigelow Aerospace put in $250 million of its founder's money and laid off all 88 staff in March 2020. Aurora Station offered 12-day stays at $9.5 million and closed without building anything. Vast's single-module Haven-1 had not been launched as of November 2026, with launch set for no earlier than the first quarter of 2027. Axiom Station, Orbital Reef and Starlab depend on NASA as main customer and funder, and none has flown or seeks self-government.

On the ISS, law on board is settled by treaty. The Intergovernmental Agreement of 1998 lets each partner keep legal control over the modules it registers and over its own citizens. A country may prosecute its own citizens. If misconduct endangers another partner's citizen or damages its module, the suspect's country must consult the affected country when asked, and the affected country may prosecute if the suspect's country agrees or gives no assurance that it will take the case to its own prosecutors (Article 22). A Crew Code of Conduct sets a chain of command.

Some ideas try to work inside this system. The ORBIS lease, discussed by Alexander Salter in 2019, is a model contract for a privately owned settlement whose residents accept rules by agreement. A country's supervision would still be required, and no settlement is known to have used it. Cloud Constellation's SpaceBelt pitched orbiting data storage outside national rules, although European data law protects residents' data even when processed elsewhere, and no launch is known to have happened. Kessler syndrome, a chain reaction of collisions predicted by two NASA scientists in 1978, adds a physical limit, because one operator's debris endangers all others and no settlement can fence off its surroundings. A seriously ill resident has to be brought back to Earth, into some country, and the Rescue Agreement returns people to the launching authority, which a self-declared state appears unable to be.

The workable version is a privately owned station, licensed and registered by one country, with residents living under its law and under private contracts. Private tokens and house rules could work inside that frame without giving independence. The rough odds given for this zone, which are judgements and not measurements, put money and building above law and holding, and recognition as a state at close to nothing.
