geo.essay:
Geostationary orbit is a single ring around Earth, directly above the equator and 35,786 kilometres up, according to the European Space Agency. A satellite in this ring travels at about 3 kilometres per second and goes around once every 23 hours and 56 minutes, which is the time Earth takes to turn. Seen from the ground, it appears to hang over one spot. Dish antennas can therefore stay pointed in one direction, and weather satellites can watch one region continuously. Three evenly spaced satellites can cover most of the planet. Only one such ring exists, which makes positions in it valuable. No person has ever lived in it.

Reaching it takes two stages. A craft first follows a long oval path that climbs to 35,786 kilometres, then fires its engine again at the top to round the path into a circle. Operating there then requires a filing by a country and a launch licence, and those two requirements are the heart of the matter.

The general law is the same as in low Earth orbit. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, bars any country from taking over outer space (Article II). A treaty country must permit and oversee private activity (Article VI), and the country that registers a craft has legal power over it (Article VIII). The treaty does not name this orbit, and it does not define where outer space begins. That gap produced the one serious attempt to claim the ring.

On 3 December 1976, eight countries on the equator, Ecuador, Colombia, Brazil, Congo, Zaire, Uganda, Kenya and Indonesia, signed the Bogotá Declaration. They called the orbit a scarce natural resource and said the part above each signer's territory fell under that country's sovereignty, meaning its full legal control. Parts above open ocean were to be shared by all nations. Their argument was that the treaty never defined outer space, so it did not cover the orbit over their land. Many of them were newly independent and objected to a system that favoured countries that already had satellites. Other countries did not accept the claim, and it won little support. The usual view is that the orbit is part of outer space and so falls under the treaty's ban, although no court has ruled on the point. Two signers kept it in their law. Colombia's constitution lists its segment of the orbit as part of the country (Article 101), and its Constitutional Court said in 2004 that the country had not given up sovereignty over it. Ecuador's 2008 constitution also asserts rights over the orbit (Article 4). How a court would treat a private station parked above either country has not been tested.

In daily practice the ring is run through radio. Every satellite needs radio frequencies to work, and two transmitters on the same frequency in the same direction spoil each other. The International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the UN agency for radio and satellite coordination, keeps order. It has 194 member countries. Its founding treaty, the ITU Constitution, says radio frequencies and orbits, including the geostationary orbit, are limited natural resources, that countries should have fair access to them, and that no station may cause harmful interference (Articles 44 and 45).

Under the ITU's Radio Regulations, a country's national authority submits notices for a planned satellite. The country then works out any conflict with other countries' satellites, and those that filed earlier generally have the stronger position. Approved frequency assignments are entered in the Master International Frequency Register, the official global list. Filings carry fees to recover the ITU's costs. People often call the result an orbital slot, which is a recorded right to use certain frequencies from a certain position. It is an entry on a list, and it is not land.

This is the obstacle that matters most. A frequency filing can only come from the national authority of a member country. A station without one would have no recorded protection from interference, and other operators would appear to have no duty to coordinate with it. A country outside the UN can join the ITU only with the agreement of two-thirds of the members, and a self-declared state would first have to persuade them that it is a country at all.

Tongasat shows both how open and how closed this system is. Matt Nilson, a businessman who had moved to Tonga, a small kingdom in the South Pacific, persuaded its king in 1987 that even a tiny country could apply. The government authorised the venture in April 1988, and in March 1990 he applied for 16 of the 180 slots then available. Intelsat, a satellite operator, and the United States objected. The ITU agreed in March 1991 after he cut the request to six, and Tonga eventually held nine. The plan was to rent each one for $2 million a year, with half the profit going to the government. Lawyers have described this as in effect a flag of convenience for space, meaning a country that lends its registration to outside operators, and later filings came from Gibraltar, Papua New Guinea and Bermuda. Tonga could do this because it is a country. China later wanted one position and Tonga gave way in exchange for aid, and on 17 August 2018 Tonga's Lord Chief Justice ruled that the company had unlawfully received over $46 million in public money. In 2019 the court made an appeal depend on a security payment of about $15,000, and how the appeal finally ended is not known.

Suppose a private group wants a small habitat in this ring. It would need a friendly member country to file for frequencies, or to rent a position that a country already holds. It would need a launch licence, which in the United States comes from the Federal Aviation Administration with insurance against harm to others of up to $500 million. It would need an entry on a register, and the Registration Convention, the treaty on listing objects launched into space, gives private people no way to do that themselves. That country then holds legal power over the habitat and everyone aboard, so the filing, the licence and the register all lead back to a government. Costs follow. A Falcon 9 rocket costs about $3,246 per kilogram to low orbit, and this ring is far higher. The habitat would sit in a crowded band and would be expected to leave at the end of its life. In 2023 the US Federal Communications Commission issued its first debris fine, to Dish Network, because its satellite EchoStar-7 ran low on fuel and stopped short of the higher "graveyard" orbit it had agreed to reach.

Everyday problems are the same as on any space station. Food at 2.77 kilograms per person per day must come from Earth, and medical care beyond first aid means a return trip. Crime falls under the registering country and under each person's home country. Americans still owe US tax returns.

Misunderstandings tend to centre on the word "slot". Holding one gives no sovereignty, no right to exclude anyone physically, and no standing as a state. The Bogotá claim is also misread as a live rule, when only two constitutions keep it and other countries have not accepted it. Standing directly over an equatorial country does not place a station under that country's law, except in the eyes of that country.

The most workable version is an ordinary licensed station, registered by a cooperating country, using frequencies that country has filed or rented. Tonga's experience suggests a small country may be willing to act as the filing partner for a fee. A private group would still need that country to apply for it, and would stay under its law and its power to withdraw. The rough odds given for this zone, which are judgements and not measurements, put building here at about 3 percent and holding out against outside control at about 15 percent, because the station depends on its filing country for radio protection and on its licence to operate.

mars-and-beyond.essay:
Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun, about half the size of Earth, with a day of 24.6 hours and a year of 687 Earth days. It is a cold, dusty desert with a very thin atmosphere, mostly carbon dioxide. Temperatures range from about 20 C down to about -153 C. It has no global magnetic field, and its atmosphere offers little protection from falling rocks. Water exists mainly as ice just under the surface in the polar regions. Only robots have ever been there. Its distance is the main thing to examine in law and in practice. A radio message takes several minutes each way, and at times more than 20, so no one on Mars can hold a live conversation with Earth.

The legal starting point is the same as for the Moon. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, covers natural bodies in space generally, and nothing in it stops at the Moon's orbit. No country may take over a planet by claiming authority, by use or occupation, or by any other means (Article II). A country must authorise and keep overseeing private activity (Article VI). The country that registered a craft has legal power over it and its people, with no mention of any distance where this ends (Article VIII). Countries must also avoid contaminating other worlds (Article IX). For the countries that have joined it, the Moon Agreement, a separate treaty with few members, extends to all bodies in the solar system other than Earth (Article 1).

There is also a scientific rulebook. COSPAR, an international committee of space scientists, keeps a Policy on Planetary Protection, an international standard on keeping other worlds free of contamination from Earth, last revised in January 2026. It works through national space agencies and has no treaty force of its own. A licensing country could still apply it to a private mission as a way of meeting its duty under the Outer Space Treaty.

The machines already on Mars show how property works there. The Soviet probe Mars 3 made the first soft landing in December 1971 and failed 110 seconds later. It remains Russian property today. NASA's Viking 1 lander of 1976, Phoenix of 2008 and InSight of 2018 sit silent, and they still belong to the United States. So do the rovers Curiosity and Perseverance, including the sealed sample tubes Perseverance left on the ground for a later mission. China's Tianwen-1 lander and Zhurong rover remain China's after dust covered Zhurong's solar panels and it failed to wake in December 2022. In each case the country owns the machine and gains no title to the ground.

The best-known attempt to write a different rule came from a private company. In October 2020 the test-phase customer terms for Starlink, SpaceX's satellite internet service, said that for services on Mars or in transit there "the parties recognize Mars as a free planet and that no Earth-based government has authority or sovereignty over Martian activities", with disputes settled "through self-governing principles". A term in a private contract binds only the people who signed it. It cannot release SpaceX from the United States, which under the treaty must authorise and supervise it. An article in Völkerrechtsblog, an international law blog, argued that SpaceX's conduct in space counts as that of the United States, and that such a claim risks breaching the ban on taking over a planet. A note at the University of Richmond said the clause tried to sidestep international law. No court has tested the clause, and it is not known whether later versions of the terms keep it.

Suppose a private group plans a settlement. Before departure it needs a launching country, an entry on a register and a licence. That country is responsible for the group and in legal control of what it registers. Next comes timing. Earth and Mars come nearest about every 26 months, so ships leave in batches. China's Tianwen-1 took from 23 July 2020 to 10 February 2021 to reach Mars orbit, a little over six months. Radio frequencies come through the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency whose members are countries.

Money is where the real attempts have failed. Mars One, a small Dutch venture announced in 2012 by Bas Lansdorp, planned a one-way colony paid for partly by a reality television show, at an estimated $6 billion for the first mission. It said 202,586 people applied, while Joseph Roche, a physicist among the finalists, said only 2,761 had completed the process, and the company later confirmed his figure. On 15 January 2019 the Civil Court of Basel in Switzerland declared Mars One Ventures bankrupt with debts of about 1 million euros. No hardware was built. The Mars Society, founded by the engineer Robert Zubrin in 1998, is a volunteer nonprofit whose physical work has all been on Earth, at simulated Mars bases on Devon Island in Canada and in the desert. It held contests on designing a colony of 1,000 and a city state of one million, with a $10,000 prize for the second, and it has adopted no known constitution for Mars. Elon Musk's stated hope, as reported by Universe Today, is 1,000 Starship rockets carrying 100 people per trip every 26 months, toward a million people. Such a transport system does not yet exist.

A 2020 model by the researcher Salotti in the journal Scientific Reports estimates about 110 as the minimum for a self-sustaining colony, by comparing the work required for survival with the time people have available. It holds only under the model's assumptions. No project has produced its own food at scale. Each person needs about 0.84 kilograms of oxygen a day, and space station crews used food at 2.77 kilograms per person per day, so a failed harvest would be a serious emergency when the next ship might be two years away.

Daily life brings its own bumps. No hospital would be near. Astronauts of member countries must assist each other (Article V), which helps only if another crew happens to be there. A crime would fall under the registering country and under home countries, and US law reaches offences by or against US nationals outside any nation. American settlers would still owe US tax returns every year. Children born there would take whatever nationality their parents' countries give, since the treaty does not mention birth, and whether its words about "personnel" cover a child born on Mars is not settled.

Paper claims appear here too, and they fail for the same reasons as elsewhere. In 1997 three men in Yemen complained to their Prosecutor General that NASA had invaded Mars, which they said they inherited from ancestors 3,000 years earlier. A popular history newsletter says the complaint was rejected, and no court record is known. Deed sellers also offer plots on Mars. The International Institute of Space Law, a professional body of space lawyers, has warned that such deeds can mislead buyers.

The most common misunderstanding is that distance removes the law. Distance slows enforcement, since no navy could arrive in less than months. In law, the registering country's power continues, and a settlement relying on ships from Earth would also depend on whoever licenses those ships. The rough odds given for this zone, which are judgements and not measurements, reflect this by putting holding on at about 35 percent, and recognition as a state at about 0.2 percent. The usual test in the Montevideo Convention of 1933 asks for a defined territory, and the Outer Space Treaty denies one.

The most workable version is a settlement licensed and registered by a supportive country, with local rules agreed among residents by contract, and growing self-reliance that gives it more practical freedom over time. The same odds put building even that within 25 years at about 2 percent. Its legal status would remain that of a registered outpost.

terra-nullius-land.essay:
Nearly all the dry land on Earth is claimed by some country. A few small pieces appear not to be, and the two most famous are Bir Tawil, between Egypt and Sudan, and Gornja Siga, on the Danube between Croatia and Serbia. A much larger piece, Marie Byrd Land in Antarctica, is unclaimed too, under the separate rules of the Antarctic Treaty. Some people conclude that they can go to such places, plant a flag and start a country. That idea rests on an old legal term.

Terra nullius is Latin for land belonging to no one. In international law it is a technical term for how countries acquire land. It concerns sovereignty, a country's authority over a place, which is different from owning a plot under a country's property law. The International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, described it in its Western Sahara opinion of 1975 as land that can be acquired by occupation (paragraph 79). Occupation in this classic sense is something countries do, so an individual's flag appears not to be enough on a reading of that passage.

Two older rulings show what was expected. In the Island of Palmas case of 1928, Max Huber held that discovery gives only a starting claim, and that the continuous and peaceful display of the functions of a state is as good as a title. In the Clipperton case of 1931, the arbitrator held that on a completely uninhabited island a state's clear intention, public notice and brief presence could be enough. Those rulings describe governments competing. Western Sahara added a limit. Countries at the relevant time did not treat land inhabited by tribes or peoples with social and political organization as terra nullius, and the Court applied that to Western Sahara's nomadic peoples (paragraphs 80 and 81).

Bir Tawil exists because of two lines drawn under British control, a straight political line of 1899 and an irregular administrative line of 1902. Egypt relies on the first and Sudan on the second, because each line gives that country the more valuable Halaib Triangle. Under either position Bir Tawil, 2,060 km² of desert, belongs to the other, so neither claims it. It has no water source and can be reached only through Egypt or Sudan. People also use it, including the Ababda people according to one academic paper, and migrants from Sudan dig for gold there. Under the Western Sahara reasoning, that use weakens any description of the land as empty.

On 16 June 2014 Jeremiah Heaton, a Virginia farmer, planted a flag there and declared the Kingdom of North Sudan so that his daughter could be a princess. He said he asked permission in Cairo for the trip, he applied for UN observer status, and he offered titles for $25. Suyash Dixit of India drove in on 4 November 2017 and declared the Kingdom of Dixit, and others announced a Kingdom of Middle Earth and a Kingdom of the Yellow Mountain. These rival private claimants have no court to settle anything between them, because only states can hold title to territory in international law. No one has settled there and no government recognizes any of them.

Gornja Siga is about 7 km² of forest and floodplain on the west bank of the Danube. The border was drawn by a 1947 commission whose conclusions were never made law. Serbia places the border on the river's navigable channel. Croatia follows old land records from before the river shifted westward, which give it areas on the far bank that Serbia holds. Those same records leave Gornja Siga on the Serbian side, while Serbia's river line leaves it on the Croatian side. So each country treats it as the other's. Both call this a border dispute, which is different from giving the land up, so whether it belongs to no one is contested. Croatian police patrol the area.

On 13 April 2015 the Czech politician Vit Jedlicka declared the Free Republic of Liberland there, and it attracted hundreds of thousands of citizenship applications. Croatian police have detained and fined people entering, and one was sentenced to 15 days in prison. In August 2023 supporters built wooden shelters. Police arrested Jedlicka on 9 September, and on 21 September a private company removed the camp under police watch. The Free Republic of Verdis, on a neighbouring 128-acre strip, tried a camp in October 2023. Its founder says Croatia destroyed it within days and banned him permanently. The Kingdom of Enclava was declared in 2015 by a Polish tourist on a plot between Slovenia and Croatia, after he read online that it was unclaimed. Slovenia's foreign ministry said the plot was part of a claim going to international arbitration. The Sapodilla Cayes, a small uninhabited atoll run by Belize, are in a case at the International Court of Justice between Belize and Honduras, and Guatemala has been allowed to take part.

Suppose a person tries Gornja Siga. The first bump is the border, since reaching it means crossing Croatian or Serbian controls. Croatia says visitors must obey Croatian law, so the person faces detention, a fine and possibly an entry ban. At Bir Tawil, the first bump is passing through Egypt or Sudan, then water, food and fuel carried from there. The next bumps are the same at both sites. Banks need a recognized supervisor and treaties run only between states. A passport from such a place is a novelty that may bring charges if used at a border. US citizens still owe tax on worldwide income. Children's birth records and any inheritance would run through the parents' home countries. Money can still be raised from a distance. Verdis reported about 15,000 applications at $16 each, and Liberland reported about 6,000 paying e-residents.

History does contain self-governing places in such gaps, and they lasted only while their neighbours tolerated them. Cospaia, created in 1440 by a treaty that named a creek when two creeks had the same name, held about 250 people. Florence and the Papal States accepted it in 1484 because that was cheaper than redrawing the line, and their successors divided it in 1826. Couto Misto, three villages on the Spain-Portugal border, paid tax to neither until the Treaty of Lisbon of 1864. Neutral Moresnet, 3.5 km² around a zinc mine, was set up by the Netherlands and Prussia in 1816 and run by their commissioners, grew from 256 to 4,668 people, and ended with Germany's annexation in 1915. Bottleneck, a strip left between Allied occupation zones in Germany, ran itself with about 17,000 people from 1919 to 1920 until German rule returned. Kowloon Walled City held about 33,000 people on 2.6 hectares because Britain and China each declined to act, and they demolished it once they agreed to.

Other gaps closed by force. Indian Stream, settlers in land claimed by both the US and Britain, declared independence in 1832 to stop paying tax twice, and New Hampshire's militia ended it in 1835. No Man's Land, the present Oklahoma panhandle, had thousands of settlers and a government called Cimarron Territory, and Congress refused to recognize it and joined the strip to Oklahoma Territory in 1890. Jonathan Lambert declared himself ruler of Tristan da Cunha in 1810 or 1811, drowned in 1812, and Britain took the islands in 1816 by sending a garrison.

A common misunderstanding concerns the Montevideo Convention, the 1933 treaty whose definition of a state is the usual checklist. It says a state's political existence does not depend on recognition by others (Article 3). It still requires a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to enter relations with other states (Article 1). In its Kosovo opinion of 2010 (paragraph 84) the Court found that general international law contains no applicable ban on declarations of independence. That is a narrow point, and the Court did not say that a declaration creates a state.

A claim can operate as an online community, a publicity project or a legal experiment, with its members living elsewhere, as Liberland's do on houseboats and in a village on the Serbian side. Permanent settlement has not been achieved at either site. The older cases suggest that a lasting arrangement would need the neighbouring countries' agreement, which none of Egypt, Sudan, Croatia or Serbia has offered.

digital-no-territory.essay:
A digital country is a group of people who organise online and call themselves a nation, with no land of their own. Founders like the idea because the projects that held land are the ones that met arrests and raids. Anyone can found one for the cost of a website.

The difficulty lies in where the members and machines actually are. Each participant stays under the law of the place they live, and each server sits under the law of the place it stands. A person in Ohio who joins an online nation still pays US taxes and still needs a US passport to travel. John Perry Barlow's Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace, published on 8 February 1996, told governments they had no sovereignty, meaning legal authority, online. It created no institutions, and governments have since acted against its claim, because servers and the people who run them are within their reach.

The legal test comes from the Montevideo Convention, a 1933 treaty whose definition of a state is the usual checklist. It asks for a defined territory (Article 1). It also says statehood does not depend on recognition (Article 3), and reading the two together appears to keep the territory test in place. A project with no land therefore fails one of the four tests, and it can still function as an association, a company or a club.

Suppose a group now tries to act like a country. A web domain ending in a country code follows the ISO 3166 list, the international list of country codes, under a 1994 document called RFC 1591, and IANA, the body that manages these domains, says it does not decide what is a country. Passports follow the standard of the International Civil Aviation Organization, the UN agency for civil flying, and its Doc 9303 takes issuer codes from the ISO 3166 agency or from separately listed organisations. A project on neither list has no code for a border machine to read. In 2002 a group travelling on passports of Elgaland-Vargaland, a Swedish art project in the form of a country, was detained in Estonia and sent back to Sweden the next day.

The next bump is money. Selling citizenship, land or tokens to the public brings securities law, the law on investments sold to the public, along with fraud law. Moving money brings the rules set by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), the international body that writes anti-money-laundering standards. Banks and crypto exchanges apply those rules to members at the point where tokens turn into ordinary money. A project also needs a real company to hold its bank account, which puts it under that company's home law. CityDAO, which bought 40 acres in Wyoming for about $100,000 in 2021, chose Wyoming because it was then the only state letting a group run through software on a blockchain, a shared public ledger, hold property as a company. Its 6,500 or so citizens in June 2022 were token holders, zoning may allow only one house on each 40-acre lot, and in May 2023 the land was undeveloped.

A country with no location is also easy to fake. The Dominion of Melchizedek, declared in 1990 by Mark Pedley, claimed a Colombian island, a shoal that appears to have been invented and part of Antarctica, among other places. About 300 bank licences were claimed to have been sold by the end of the 1990s, and one scheme took over $4 million from at least 1,400 people. The Marshall Islands condemned its claims in 1998, and Pedley pleaded guilty to share manipulation in 2010.

Other projects fade or stay small. Bitnation, founded in 2014, offered blockchain ID cards and had about 25 volunteer embassies in 2016. With no recognition, an embassy could do little for an asylum seeker, and by August 2022 its domain had been sold. Wirtland, founded in 2008, claimed about 700 citizens and proposed asking Nauru for territory, and no land is known to have changed hands. Afropolitan raised $2.1 million as a digital nation for the African diaspora and, according to a critical 2025 article, was running a podcast and three services three years on. Asgardia reported more than 290,000 citizens in March 2019, and its only territory, a 2.8-kilogram satellite under US authority, burned up in 2022. A list of free sign-ups differs from the permanent population the test asks for, since those people live and pay tax elsewhere.

Virtual land is a separate misunderstanding. Decentraland sold plots as tokens, with one sale of $2.43 million in 2021, and fewer than 1,000 users a day were making transactions in October 2022. A token gives no authority over any place on Earth. A virtual city designed in 2022 for Liberland, a self-declared country on the Danube, gave it no access to the real land, which Croatia controls. Real governments have tried the same idea without any change in law. Sweden spent 400,000 kronor, about $57,000, on a Second Life embassy in 2007, which added nothing to its legal status, and it is not known whether the metaverse embassy Barbados planned in 2021 ever opened.

Balaji Srinivasan's 2022 book on the network state proposes an online community that buys scattered land and eventually seeks diplomatic recognition. Its test site was the Network School, in a hotel in Johor, Malaysia. Officers checked 266 foreigners there on 14 July 2026 and found all documents valid. On 21 July the city council revoked its business licence, and it moved to Astana, Kazakhstan, under a non-binding memorandum. Praxis, a New York company, reported $525 million, of which $500 million is conditional on listing tokens, and it has looked at Greenland, a California base and Uruguay. No Praxis city has been built. A group that holds a building holds it under a local licence, and that licence can be withdrawn.

The cases that succeed have a real state or a long history behind them. Estonia's e-Residency gives foreigners a digital identity for running Estonian companies, with over 144,000 e-residents from 187 countries. It gives no citizenship or right to live there, and it relies on Estonia's territory, law, courts and banks. Estonia's data embassy is a Tier 4 (highest-reliability grade) data centre in Luxembourg holding state databases, by agreement between the two countries, drawing on the treaty on embassies, the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations. Tuvalu, a recognised country of about 10,000 people, has asked other countries to agree in advance that it stays a state if the sea takes its land. Twenty-six had reportedly done so by December 2023, and in 2025 the International Court of Justice said the loss of one part of a state "would not necessarily entail the loss of its statehood". The question has not been tested. The Nansen passport of 1922, a travel paper for refugees, worked because governments agreed in advance to honour it. Garry Davis's World Passport, issued from 1953 for a fee, had no such agreement, and he was regularly arrested and expelled.

The Sovereign Military Order of Malta is often cited as proof that land is unnecessary. It lost Malta to Napoleon in 1798, kept its status, and reports relations with 118 countries. It began in the 11th century and was already treated as sovereign when it lost its land, a history a new group cannot copy.

Borrowing a real state's protection has also failed. In 2010 the Swedish Pirate Party offered to host The Pirate Bay inside parliament for legal cover, and it won no seats.

The most workable version is candid about what it is. It is a company, nonprofit or membership club registered in a real country, with no securities sold, no passports for border use, ordinary tax compliance by members and a clear statement that citizenship is membership. It can last, with culture, voting and shared funds, and there is no single place for a government to raid. It holds no land, its members and servers remain under local law, and recognition as a state remains close to nil.

iso-3166.what:
Computers and clerks around the world need short, agreed labels for countries. ISO 3166 is the international list of two- and three-letter country codes, used by banks, shipping, airlines, web domains and passports. France is FR, for example. When a bank's software asks which country a customer lives in, it usually picks from this list. A place that is missing from it can run into trouble at the most ordinary moments, since many forms and systems have no box for it.

The list has 249 codes assigned. A body called ISO, the International Organization for Standardization, publishes the standard, and an office called the Maintenance Agency keeps the list. The agency relies on someone else's judgment of who is a country. The only way in is to be registered in either the UN Terminology Bulletin Country Names or the UN Statistics Division's Standard Country or Area Codes. Entry therefore depends on the UN. The rule is widely reported in these terms, although the exact wording in the agency's own documents may differ.

A founder cannot apply and persuade the agency directly. The practical sequence starts at the UN lists, and a self-declared place has no way to reach those lists on its own.

Kosovo shows how an accepted place copes without a code. It uses XK, a code from the 'user-assigned' range, which sits outside the official list. Those codes exist for private use, and organizations can agree among themselves to treat one as meaning a place. That works only because the organizations choose to go along, and Kosovo's recognition by 110 UN members gives them a reason. A micronation can type any letters it likes into its own website, and outside systems have no reason to accept them.

iso-4217.what:
Banks do not write out "United States dollar" when they record a payment. They use a three-letter code, USD, from an international list called ISO 4217. EUR is the euro. These codes matter because banks and trading systems use them to book payments, and the software that does this expects each amount to carry a code it recognizes.

SIX, the Swiss exchange group, is the official Maintenance Agency for the list, meaning the office that keeps it, and calls itself the only recognized, authoritative source on currency codes. The purpose is practical. If every bank used its own label, payments between banks would keep failing or going to the wrong currency.

Suppose a new place prints its own notes. Without a code, its currency would have no standard listing on normal payment systems. A bank in Frankfurt would have no standard way to book a payment in it. That appears to limit the currency to local paper money or a private token. Sealand has issued coins since 1972, nominally pegged 1:1 to the US dollar, and the micronation Atlantium sold coins and banknotes in its imperial solidus. Both are self-issued money of that local or collectable kind.

The terms on who may request a code are set by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), which publishes the standard, and are not spelled out in the agency's public description, so they are hard to state with confidence. In practice the code is a small part of the problem, because a code alone gives no bank a reason to deal in the currency. Banks would still want a licensed central authority behind it and a way to swap it for other money.

fatf-travel-rule.what:
When money moves between banks, governments want to be able to follow it, so that criminals and terrorists cannot hide behind anonymous transfers. The Financial Action Task Force (FATF), an international body, writes the standard that most countries' anti-money-laundering rules follow. FATF is not a court and does not arrest anyone. Its members write the standard, and countries then turn it into national law, which their banks must obey.

Its Recommendation 16, known as the Travel Rule, requires financial institutions and virtual asset service providers (crypto businesses) to share who sent and who receives a transfer. The information travels with the payment, like a label on a parcel. For cross-border transfers above USD/EUR 1,000, the 2025 revision requires the name, account number and country and town of the person receiving the money. The revisions take effect at the end of 2030 and reach crypto firms indirectly, through FATF's Recommendation 15 on new technologies. FATF planned further guidance on these changes, and each country's law may differ in detail when it is written.

For a founder, this has an effect that is easy to miss. A resident of a self-declared place who receives a transfer must give a name, an account and a country and town. A place the bank's system does not list may not be accepted, so the person's real legal address comes into the record. A bank or crypto business that cannot get the information has a reason to refuse the transfer.

Holding crypto does not remove this, because the rule covers the businesses that convert it. A project that promises members financial privacy from every government is promising something its banking partners cannot lawfully provide, and its members meet the rule each time money enters or leaves through a regulated firm.

correspondent-banking.what:
A bank in a small town cannot have an account at every bank in the world. So banks use a chain. International payments travel between banks that hold accounts with each other, called correspondent banks. A payment from a village in one country to a shop in another may pass through two or three of them, usually including a large bank in New York or London for dollars and pounds.

Each bank in the chain is legally answerable for what passes through it, so it wants to know who is at the other end. It relies on the other country's banking law and supervisor to have checked the customer. A new place with no banking law or supervisor gives them no one to rely on.

The Financial Stability Board, an international body that monitors the financial system, reports a steady fall in those relationships. Active correspondents dropped 3.9% in 2016, 4.1% in 2017 and 3.4% in 2018, with US dollar links falling fastest and smaller, higher-risk places hit hardest. This retreat is called de-risking. These figures stop at 2018, and later years may show a different pace. Even recognized small countries have been cut off, so a place with no recognition starts behind them.

Without a correspondent, your people cannot receive a wire transfer. A founder would need a bank in a real country willing to serve the project as an ordinary customer, under that country's rules. Members would keep their accounts in their home countries. Melchizedek claimed to have sold about 300 bank licences by the end of the 1990s, and in 1991 shell banks tried to get loans with fake securities and were shut down, which helps explain why banks treat licences from self-declared places with such suspicion.

swift.what:
SWIFT is the messaging network banks use to instruct payments. It describes itself as a member-owned cooperative under Belgian law, serving more than 12,500 institutions in over 200 countries and territories. When one bank tells another to pay out money, the instruction usually travels over this network in a standard format, much as a telegram once did. It carries the messages between banks, and the money itself moves through the accounts banks hold with each other.

Because so many international payments depend on these messages, governments have treated access as a form of power. Regional law binds SWIFT, and it says that as a Belgian company it must follow EU regulation. In March 2012 an EU regulation made it disconnect sanctioned Iranian banks. In March 2022, an EU regulation banned the service for seven Russian banks. A network that large would not be able to ignore such an order, and a bank removed from it has to find slower and costlier ways to pay.

SWIFT sets its own eligibility criteria. The practical path for a new place is a licensed bank, which needs a licensing authority other countries accept. Suppose a founder sets up a "national bank" on a platform and asks to join. The first question would be which authority licensed and supervises it. A self-appointed ministry's stamp gives no answer that another bank's compliance office can accept. Melchizedek's bank licences, about 300 claimed sold by the end of the 1990s, show why that question gets asked.

Crypto payment systems avoid SWIFT, and they then run into the exchange and stablecoin rules described in the other entries. At the point where members want to turn tokens into the local money for rent or food, a regulated business and a bank are usually involved again. In practice a project's members would use their existing accounts in real countries, which reach SWIFT through those banks, and they would remain under those banks' rules.

fatf-grey.what:
Banks need a quick way to judge how risky a country is. The Financial Action Task Force (FATF), the international body that sets anti-money-laundering standards, provides one by listing places with weak rules. It reviews countries' laws and enforcement, and those with serious gaps go on a list officially called jurisdictions under increased monitoring and widely known as the grey list. A country on the list agrees to a plan to fix the gaps, and it comes off when the gaps are closed.

The list has real costs. A paper at the International Monetary Fund by Kida and Paetzold estimates that being on this 'grey list' cuts capital inflows by about 7.6% of GDP, the yearly value of a country's economy. Banks and investors treat the listing as a warning, and they demand more checks or leave.

After the June 2026 meeting, 22 places were on the list. Four came off in October 2026 (Bulgaria, Monaco, Côte d'Ivoire and DR Congo), which left 18 according to compliance firms' copies of the list. Iran, North Korea and Myanmar are on a separate high-risk list.

A self-declared place faces a different and perhaps harder position. A place FATF has never assessed would appear to have no clean record to show banks. It cannot point to a review it passed, and to a bank's compliance office an unknown place may look worse than a listed one. Building the machinery that would satisfy a reviewer takes laws, a financial intelligence office, supervisors and prosecutors, which a small project does not have. A founder would have to depend on a bank in a real country and that country's standing, with the project's members treated as higher-risk customers.

camouflage-passports.what:
Some travel documents are not forgeries of real passports and are not valid either. A camouflage passport looks real but names a country or body that does not exist. A fantasy passport is a similar novelty, not valid for travel. The difference from a real passport is simple, because no government stands behind either one and no other government has agreed to honour it.

These documents draw two kinds of buyers. Some want a souvenir of a project they like. Others hope to pass a border or open a bank account, and that is where criminal risk begins. Sealand's passports have been described as fantasy passports in a Council of the EU glossary. In 1997, the Bates family, who run Sealand, revoked them after finding an international money-laundering ring using them. The Dominion of Melchizedek sold passports for up to $3,500, and three people posing as its officials were arrested in the Philippines in 1998. A listing does not always mean fraud. The Haudenosaunee passport, issued by a people with a long claim of their own, is also listed by the European Union as a fantasy passport.

The legal risk does not depend on copying a real country's passport. In US law it is a crime to falsely make 'any passport or instrument purporting to be a passport' intended for use, and to use one (18 USC 1543). Using one at a border may bring charges under such laws, and the person also faces being refused entry and sent back.

A founder who wants to issue documents safely would label them plainly as commemorative or membership cards, would never suggest they work for travel, and would warn members not to present them to any officer. Members still need their real passports for every actual trip.

fatca-crs.what:
A person might hope that moving money offshore hides it from the tax office at home. For many people that stopped being true some years ago. Countries now get account information directly from foreign banks, under two main systems, one American and one international.

Foreign banks report US account holders to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), the US tax agency, under the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA). Americans must also report foreign financial assets above set limits. The general limit on Form 8938 is $50,000, which may be higher in some cases, and failing to report carries a $10,000 penalty. So the same account may be reported twice, once by the bank and once by the customer, and the two reports can be matched.

Many other countries swap account data under the Common Reporting Standard of the OECD, a club of mostly wealthy countries. Banks collect each customer's tax home, and governments send the data to one another. A report on the Global Forum, the international group that oversees this exchange, gives 171 million accounts worth nearly EUR 13 trillion, 172 member countries and territories, and about EUR 135 billion in extra revenue. These figures are as given in trade press coverage of the report and are best read as approximate.

Your bank therefore tells your home tax office you have the account, whichever flag you live under. A founder cannot change this by issuing a new passport, because a bank that opens an account asks for a real tax residence and proof of it. Claiming to be tax resident in a micronation gives the bank nothing it can accept, and a refusal or more questions are likely. A project running its own "bank" outside these systems would have no correspondent bank to reach the outside world. The practical result is that members remain visible to their home countries for as long as they keep money in ordinary banks.

food-water-power.what:
A settlement outside every country still needs to eat. Declarations do not touch this problem, and supply is usually what ties a project back to the nearest port. No project is known to have produced its own food at scale.

The numbers for space show how much is at stake. A person needs about 0.84 kg of oxygen a day, according to NASA, and food use on the International Space Station (ISS) ran at 2.77 kg per crew member per day. The ISS has reached 98% water recovery, and it still relies on deliveries for tanks, water bags and food. The station has government budgets behind it and still depends on deliveries, so a private group should not assume it can do without them.

At sea, a platform needs a port. Fuel, spare parts, food and people arrive by boat, and the boat must leave from somewhere. Oceanix's Busan design, a planned floating district in South Korea, intends to make its own energy on site, though that remains a plan.

Dependence on a neighbor's port appears to give that neighbor leverage. Italy blockaded Rose Island after seizing it, to stop anyone from returning. Britain's 1967 law against pirate radio made it illegal for British subjects to supply such stations, and the Dutch banned supplying them from land in 1974. Radio Caroline's broadcasts at sea stopped in 1990 for lack of fuel and supplies. A neighbour does not have to send a warship. It can act against the suppliers on its own shore.

A founder would need to count the daily tonnage, contract with suppliers in a real country and accept that country's rules on what can be shipped. Farming and desalination can reduce dependence over time. Those systems still need parts that come from elsewhere.

cost-orbit.what:
Getting anything into space costs money for every kilogram, because rockets burn huge amounts of fuel to lift it. That price sets the budget for everything else, so space planners count in dollars per kilogram.

The price has fallen a great deal. Jones, writing for NASA, calculated $54,500 per kg for the Space Shuttle to low orbit, and $2,720 per kg for SpaceX's Falcon 9 rocket at its 2018 price of $62 million. By early 2026, a full Falcon 9 for one customer was about $74 million, or $3,246 per kg at full capacity. A shared flight starts at $350,000 for 50 kg. Filings by the space company Voyager imply $90 million for a Starship flight, once certified, on one financial writer's reading of them. The words once certified matter, since that figure is a projection.

Those are rocket costs alone. Food, at 2.77 kg a day, comes to about 1,000 kg a person each year, or about $3.3 million at the Falcon 9 rate, by simple arithmetic. That is one person's food for one year, before water, air, spare parts, medicine, the habitat itself or the crew's own flight.

A founder has to compare these figures with what backers can pay. Mars One estimated $6 billion for its first mission, built no hardware, and its company was declared bankrupt in 2019 with debts of about 1 million euros. MirCorp paid for one flight to the Mir station in 2000 and ran out of money when the dot-com crash hit its main backer. Asgardia's actual reach in orbit was a single 2.8-kilogram satellite. Every launch also comes with the licensing and insurance duties of the launching country, and a cheaper ride leaves those rules in place.

cost-station.what:
Living in orbit means keeping a sealed building in working order, with air, water, power and repairs, far from any shop. The running cost of that building is much larger than most people expect. The International Space Station (ISS) costs about $3 billion a year to run, according to NASA's Inspector General. It has many governments paying for it. A private settlement would have to pay in some other way, or build far smaller.

Private companies are now testing the market. Vast, a private space station company, has committed more than $1 billion to its single-module Haven-1 station, which has slipped to no earlier than the first quarter of 2027, and it had sold no crew seat when that delay was reported. So a billion dollars has gone in before the first paying visitor.

The price of a visit gives another measure. Axiom, a private space company, gave a price of $55 million a seat for a 10-day trip to the ISS, plus NASA charges reported then as $2,000 per person per day for food and more for support. Those prices assume short stays, and a person who wanted to live in orbit would pay for flights, supplies and a share of the structure year after year.

Earlier ventures show what can happen. MirCorp signed up the paying passenger Dennis Tito and said it had $100 million in future business, but its money ran out and Mir was brought down from orbit in March 2001. Tito flew to the ISS instead.

A founder would also need a launching country's licence and registration, so the money would buy a home under that country's power. At these prices, private stays in orbit have been short trips for very wealthy people.

tuvalu-digital-nation.story:
Tuvalu is a recognised Pacific country of about 10,000 people, spread over low-lying islands that the United Nations Development Programme classes as extremely vulnerable to climate change. The Rising Nations Initiative says that small island nations such as Tuvalu, Kiribati and the Marshall Islands are likely to become uninhabitable within a few decades. That raises a question international law has never had to answer, which is what happens to a country when its land goes under water.
The usual test for a state, set out in the 1933 Montevideo Convention, asks for a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the ability to deal with other states. Territory is on that list. So on one reading Tuvalu could lose its legal existence along with its homes.
At the COP27 climate conference in November 2022 its Foreign Minister, Simon Kofe, appeared in a video standing knee deep in the ocean. He said the country would move its land, ocean and culture to the cloud, as what it called the first digital nation. The plan, part of the Future Now Project, is to map all 124 islands and islets and to record cultural objects, language, elders' stories and dances, so that people abroad and future generations can keep them.
The legal step is the more important one. Tuvalu has asked other countries to agree in advance that it stays a state whatever happens to its land. Australia's Law Society Journal reported that 26 countries, including New Zealand and Australia, had legally recognised its digital statehood by December 2023, with a goal of 50. Australia also offered residency to 280 Tuvaluans a year. In its climate advisory opinion of July 2025 the International Court of Justice, the United Nations' top court, said that the disappearance of one of a state's parts "would not necessarily entail the loss of its statehood". An advisory opinion does not bind states, though it carries weight.
The land is still there and the question has not been tested. The case differs from every self-declared internet nation in one way. Tuvalu starts as a full state with UN membership and is seeking to keep that status, so the digital record is a supplement to recognition it already has. Its strategy shows where the law's flexibility lies. States may be able to preserve a state by agreement, and this does not open the door for a new one to be created online.
